title: From AI agents to fishing dashboards: The latest stories from Unprompted, the Grafana Labs engineering blog
summary:
Some of the best technical insights come from sharing what you've built and what you've learned along the way.

That's one of the core ideas behind Unprompted, the blog we launched on Medium earlier this year to give Grafana Labs engineers and our broader OSS community a space to showcase their work. From behind-the-scenes engineering stories and technical deep dives to creative use cases for Grafana (a fishing dashboard, anyone?), it's a place to share ideas and learn from one another.

To give you a sense of what you'll find, we've rounded up a few recent posts covering everything from Grafana's architecture to monitoring your favorite reality TV show.

Behind the scenes at Grafana Labs

These posts explore some of the technical challenges our teams have tackled at Grafana Labs, including the decisions, tradeoffs, and lessons that shaped their work. 

Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding mode

Making an AI agent faster, more reliable, and less expensive takes a lot more than fine-tuning your prompts. Senior Software Engineer Dominik Broj shares how the team used production telemetry, offline evaluations, and Agent Observability to improve dashboarding mode in Grafana Assistant, reducing error rates by 73%, latency p95 by 50%, and cost by 18%.

How and why we're bringing data sources out of the Grafana monolith

Grafana data sources have historically been closely tied to the Grafana monolith. To make it easier to develop, maintain, and release data source plugins independently of Grafana's core release cycle, the team has been working to decouple them from the monolith. But what does that entail, exactly? Kate Vredenburgh, Senior Manager, Engineering, walks through it all, including the challenges of migrating existing code and how the team used AI agents to help along the way.

How we provision Grafana Play dashboards at scale with Git Sync and Terraform

Grafana Play is our public sandbox where you can explore hundreds of Grafana dashboards and dozens of data sources. It’s a great way to learn about and experiment with Grafana, but keeping all those dashboards consistent across development and production environments takes work. Senior Developer Advocate Marie Cruz shares how the team uses Git Sync (because who doesn’t love dogfooding?) and Terraform to manage dashboards as code and streamline the deployment process.

Observability tutorials and how-tos 

From troubleshooting CI/CD pipelines to monitoring Kubernetes workloads and analyzing API gateway logs, these technical how-tos offer practical guidance for tackling common observability challenges. 

How to build workload-aware SLO dashboards in Grafana for mixed Kubernetes workloads

A Kubernetes dashboard can look healthy overall, even when there are performance issues with individual workloads. In this post, community member and SRE Sai Joshitha Kathari shows how to build Grafana dashboards that account for different workload types, using Prometheus metrics, SLOs, error-budget burn rates, and alerting to get a more accurate view of reliability.

From gateway logs to actionable insights with Apache APISIX, Loki, and Grafana

API gateway logs contain valuable information about traffic, errors, and latency, but making sense of that data isn't always straightforward. In this tutorial, community member and Apache APISIX technical contributor Yilia Lin explains how to send structured logs from APISIX to Loki, then use LogQL and Grafana dashboards to identify failing routes, investigate latency, and better understand API behavior during incidents.

Troubleshooting CI/CD pipelines (and more) with OpenTelemetry traces and Grafana Cloud

When a CI/CD pipeline slows down, figuring out which steps are responsible often means piecing together timestamps from logs. Fortunately, there’s a better way. Matt Simonsen, Senior Solutions Engineer at Grafana Labs, explains how to instrument a GitHub Actions workflow with OpenTelemetry and Traces Drilldown in Grafana Cloud to make your pipeline investigations easier.

Creative and fun use cases for Grafana

Some of the most interesting Grafana use cases are also the most unexpected. Whether you’re planning your next fishing trip or want to keep closer tabs on your favorite TV show, these posts inspire fun and creative ways to use Grafana. 

Gone fishin' with Grafana Cloud: How a dashboard can help you catch more fish

Ever wished you could check all the conditions for a fishing trip in one, centralized place? Thomas Mack, Senior IT Operations Engineer at Grafana Labs, shares how to do just that with a Grafana Cloud dashboard that helps you visualize tides, wind, water temperature, and marine forecasts to decide when it's best to head out on the water.

Tracking 'The Traitors' TV show with SQL expressions in Grafana

What can a reality TV competition teach you about SQL expressions? Probably more than you think. Grafana Labs Senior Developer Advocate Simon Prickett turns his enthusiasm for “The Traitors” into a hands-on tour of SQL expressions in Grafana, combining data from Google Sheets and other sources to visualize the show’s voting patterns, eliminations, and more.

From small talk to shared stories: Building a weather dashboard for distributed teams

For distributed teams, even something as simple as talking about the weather can be a way to connect. This post, written by Yaëlle Chaudy, Senior Manager, Engineering at Grafana Labs, explores how a dashboard in Grafana Cloud can turn everyday weather data into a shared experience, giving teammates across the globe a new way to kick off conversations in their daily syncs. 

Find more stories on Unprompted

These are just a few of the stories we're sharing on Unprompted. Whether you're interested in behind-the-scenes engineering stories or simply curious about what others in the community are building, there's plenty more to explore.

Follow Unprompted on Medium for more technical deep dives, engineering lessons, and stories from the Grafana community.

Have an interesting Grafana project or technical story of your own? We're always looking for community contributors and would love to hear from you.

title: Grafana Labs’ First Executive Briefing Center Coming to Ginza
summary:
Grafana Labs does not have a headquarters office. Since its founding in 2014, it has been fully remote-first.

It began with three co-founders living on different continents, and today our team spans more than 50 countries.
From day one, the organization was designed with the assumption that everyone works remotely. Real-time meetings are kept to a minimum, information is shared through documentation, and we have cultivated a culture that trusts people to “work autonomously.” At its core lies the transparency and autonomy of open source.

And now, we are building the world’s first Executive Briefing Center (EBC) in Ginza, Tokyo.

A remote-first company creating a physical space—what does that mean?
This article is the first in a three-part series following the EBC launch project.
From the background of the concept to site selection, design philosophy, and even the demolition process, we will walk you through the journey.

Not an “office,” but an “EBC”

We do not call this place an “office.” It is an Executive Briefing Center, or EBC for short.

As a remote-first company, there is no need to commute to a fixed location every day. However, there has never been a place anywhere in the world where people can directly experience the Grafana product, or share the same physical space with customers and the community to engage with technology. The EBC is designed to serve three roles.



A place to experience the product


A space where customers can directly interact with Grafana solutions, experiencing how observability solves real challenges through demos and briefings—not through a screen, but through face-to-face conversations in the same space.



A starting point for innovation


A flexible space design that is not bound by fixed layouts, allowing the environment to adapt to different purposes and foster new ideas and use cases.

A hub for the community


A venue open for meetups and technical events, where people in the Grafana community can naturally gather and connect.


We are building the world’s first EBC in Japan—to meet the rapidly growing demand for observability in the Japanese market. And for the Grafana community that already exists here, having a physical hub carries significant meaning.

Because Grafana Labs is a company where employees around the world operate autonomously, we believe there is real value in creating a space for experiences that can only happen in person. We aim to create an open space—one where people feel that we are close to them.

Site selection — A space that embodies our culture

Two key requirements for the location

The search for a property began around April 2025. Led by Country Manager Andy Schwabecher, we explored multiple areas. There were two key requirements in the selection process.

First, the location needed to make customers feel that Grafana Labs is “right there with them.” It had to be open, accessible, and easy to drop by—a place where people could naturally engage with the Grafana solution. Not a space hidden behind security gates and reception procedures, but one that feels open and inviting. A building where customers might think, “Let’s just stop by.”

Second, the space needed to embody the way Grafana Labs works. For us, the concept of an “office” is fundamentally different from that of a typical Japanese company. It is not a place where people sit at assigned desks every day. It must be an open, flexible environment that does not contradict a remote-first way of working. It also needed to accommodate a skeleton ceiling and allow for a design that breaks away from conventional office norms.

Finding a place that satisfied both conditions was not easy.

A property once lost—and eventually secured

Around the summer of 2025, a building in Ginza was introduced by a broker. At the viewing stage, the team rated it highly, and it met all the conditions. However, during the consideration process, another tenant moved ahead, and the opportunity slipped away.

While continuing to search for other options, we received news a few months later that the original tenant had withdrawn, and the space was available again.

And so, after a long journey, we secured the current floor—about nine months after starting the search in April 2025.

Looking back, not compromising on finding a place that could physically express Grafana Labs’ culture—transparency, openness, and autonomy—was one of the most important decisions in shaping the EBC.

Design philosophy — Expressing Grafana’s culture through space

Skeleton ceiling and open interior

In a typical office or tenant space, ceilings are finished, and pipes and wiring are hidden.

At the EBC, we chose the opposite: a full skeleton ceiling. Exposed pipes and visible wiring. This itself is an expression of Grafana Labs’ philosophy of “making things visible.”

As a company whose core business is observability—the ability to see—we intentionally reflect that philosophy in the space itself.

Three areas and design principles

The space is broadly divided into three areas.

First, an area where visitors can casually experience Grafana Labs’ culture.A large screen displays content that introduces what kind of company Grafana Labs is and what we value.

Second, an area where visitors can directly experience Grafana solutions.A space where they can view demos, receive explanations, and engage in practical discussions—not through a screen, but together in the same place.

Third, private meeting rooms.Spaces designed for more in-depth conversations in a relaxed atmosphere.
Across all areas, the common design philosophy is to create a place where people can easily drop by and directly interact with Grafana Labs members. The goal is to provide a sense of comfort that helps visitors feel at ease.

Interior and flexibility

In selecting the interior layout and color scheme, we intentionally avoided the rigid feel of a typical office. Instead, we focused on creating a relaxed environment where conversations naturally emerge.
Furniture in the EBC is designed to be as movable as possible.

On a daily basis, the space includes an eight-person free-address desk (with monitors at each seat), window-side bench seating, and high tables. For meetups and community events, these can be moved to the sides, transforming the space into an open area that can accommodate gatherings of around 50 people.

Not fixed, but flexible. A space that changes form depending on its use—that is the core concept of the EBC design.

Meeting room names — Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)

Meeting room names — Amber, Jade, Mikage
There are three meeting rooms in total.
We utilized one existing room and added new partitions—retaining part of the original wall—to create three separate spaces.

For a remote-first company like Grafana Labs, having physical meeting rooms is itself a new experience.
Various ideas were considered, including place names like “Tokyo,” “Ginza,” and “Kyoto,” as well as festival-themed names like “Kanda” and “Tenjin.”

In the end, we chose names based on Japanese stones and minerals:

Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)

Minerals are formed deep underground over long periods of time. While their beauty is undeniable, what resonated most with the team was the weight of that time.

What we aim for in this space is to build long-term relationships with our customers—not one-time interactions, but connections that deepen over time.

There is also another meaning: these are names rooted in Japan. The sound itself feels familiar and naturally accepted.
As a global company, we wanted the space to feel grounded in Japan, and for that sense to be reflected even in the names.

Demolition — Walls removed, space revealed

Originally, this floor was divided into three separate rooms for different tenants. Air conditioning was already installed, making it move-in ready. To create an open, single-floor space, we began by demolishing the walls that separated the rooms. The ceiling was also replaced with a skeleton structure to better reflect Grafana’s open culture.

Floor plan before demolition: three rooms on one floor

Before demolition

After demolition

With two walls removed, the space opened up into a single, expansive area.

Current status and what’s next

As of March 2026, the demolition work has been completed.
The walls are gone, the ceiling has been stripped, and a large open floor now stretches across the space.
Structural work has been completed, and from here, full-scale interior construction based on the design will begin.

The target completion is late April.
After inspections and adjustments, operations are expected to begin in mid-May.
Starting next week, the space will begin to transform daily, with new walls, flooring, and equipment installation.

Coming next

Walls go up, floors are laid, wiring is installed, and monitors are set in place.
What once existed only on blueprints will take shape as a real, physical space.

In the next article, we will share an on-site construction report, coordination with designers and contractors, and behind-the-scenes insights into equipment selection—bringing you the reality of the build process.

title: Bring charts, queries, and context into one shareable document: Introducing Grafana Notebooks
summary:
A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures. You have an error-rate chart in your dashboard, a query that narrows the failures to one payment provider, and an explanation you've been exploring with Grafana Assistant. To bring your teammate up to speed, you start collecting screenshots and query links, then write out how they connect.

That explanation is part of the analysis. Your teammate needs to see what supports the conclusion and where you're still making an assumption. As findings come from both your own exploration in Grafana and from AI-assisted work, having one place to examine them together becomes key.

Grafana Notebooks help you do just that, bringing charts, queries, and findings from Assistant together in one working document, so teammates can follow your reasoning and assess next steps. In this post, we’ll use the checkout example above to show how this works in practice, then look at how Notebooks can support rollout decisions and post-incident reviews.

How Notebooks work: develop your analysis in a working document

Through conversations with users, we've heard a recurring need for a lightweight place to work through a question and share the results. Notebooks give that work room to develop inside Grafana, from an initial observation to a recommendation someone can assess.

You can start with a panel you've already found. Select Add to notebook from its dashboard menu, or from the Add menu in Explore, and choose a new or existing notebook. Then add your explanation and reorder the blocks as the argument takes shape. Your edits save automatically.

Assistant can contribute to your working document, too. Add a visualization generated in an Assistant conversation directly to a notebook, whether you're using the side pane or Workspace. Once you're in the notebook, open the Assistant side pane to ask for changes to a visualization or help refining the document. You can also edit the content directly as your analysis develops.

Work through a question and share your conclusion

Let's revisit the checkout example. Your notebook starts with the error-rate panel and a question: could the latest payment-service deployment explain the increase?

Alongside the panel, you bring in an Explore query that narrows the errors to requests to one payment provider. You can refine that query in the notebook without changing the source dashboard, and can also set an absolute start and end time on the error-rate panel to keep readers focused on the period around the deployment.


You ask Assistant to chart payment-provider timeouts before and after the deployment, then add the visualization directly from the conversation to your notebook. Within the notebook, you open the Assistant side pane and ask, "Break this chart down by payment provider." In this example, the breakdown shows an increase for the provider you identified in Explore. You add a detail from the deployment notes: the release changed that provider's timeout setting. You explain why that connection deserves testing.

Before sharing, you put the suspected cause and proposed test near the top, with the supporting charts and explanation below. A reader can see what you're recommending, then follow the evidence. The next step is to reproduce the behavior with the previous and current timeout settings.

You share the notebook link with the payment-service team. A teammate with access can read the analysis and examine the queries as they plan the test. Their next action happens in the service's test environment, informed by the work you've brought together.

Support rollout decisions, post-incident reviews, and more

The same approach works for questions outside troubleshooting. For example, after a deployment intended to improve performance, you could bring together latency and resource-usage charts, explain the differences you observe, and document any trade-offs. Share the notebook with the service owners to help them decide whether to expand the rollout or make another change.

For a post-incident review, a notebook can bring relevant queries together with an account of what happened. Place your explanation beside the evidence so readers can understand the conclusions before discussing follow-up work. A finding about repeated timeouts, for example, might support a proposal to change retry behavior or add a load test.

Start with a question your team needs to answer

For your first notebook, choose a question you're already working through in Grafana. Add the evidence you've found, explain what you think it means, and make the next question or recommendation clear. Share it with the people whose expertise you need.

We're also exploring richer collaboration in Notebooks, including comments and live editing. Our ambition is to give people and agents more ways to develop their work together, with the evidence and discussion in the same place.

Notebooks are in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, as of the Grafana 13.3 release. Grafana Cloud access is rolling out over the coming weeks. 

For self-managed Grafana, follow the Notebooks guide to enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. Once available, create a notebook from the Notebooks page. You can also start with findings from an Assistant conversation.

A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures. You have an error-rate chart in your dashboard, a query that narrows the failures to one payment provider, and an explanation you've been exploring with Grafana Assistant. To bring your teammate up to speed, you start collecting screenshots and query links, then write out how they connect.

That explanation is part of the analysis. Your teammate needs to see what supports the conclusion and where you're still making an assumption. As findings come from both your own exploration in Grafana and from AI-assisted work, having one place to examine them together becomes key.

Grafana Notebooks help you do just that, bringing charts, queries, and findings from Assistant together in one working document, so teammates can follow your reasoning and assess next steps. In this post, we’ll use the checkout example above to show how this works in practice, then look at how Notebooks can support rollout decisions and post-incident reviews.

How Notebooks work: develop your analysis in a working document

Through conversations with users, we've heard a recurring need for a lightweight place to work through a question and share the results. Notebooks give that work room to develop inside Grafana, from an initial observation to a recommendation someone can assess.

You can start with a panel you've already found. Select Add to notebook from its dashboard menu, or from the Add menu in Explore, and choose a new or existing notebook. Then add your explanation and reorder the blocks as the argument takes shape. Your edits save automatically.

Assistant can contribute to your working document, too. Add a visualization generated in an Assistant conversation directly to a notebook, whether you're using the side pane or Workspace. Once you're in the notebook, open the Assistant side pane to ask for changes to a visualization or help refining the document. You can also edit the content directly as your analysis develops.

title: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs
summary:
A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out.

Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly.

To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. 

“When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.”

In this post, we’ll explore how full-text search speeds up log investigations. You can also learn more in the ObservabilityCON 2026 talk below.

Why labels alone only get you so far

Historically, Loki only indexed labels, then scanned every line in the selected streams. That is fast when the selector and the time range are already narrow. Searching a wide selector over a long window for one request ID means reading all of those lines. If you've run Loki at scale, you've probably reached for one of these techniques to avoid that scan:

  • Put the whole or partial ID in a label. This is an obvious fix, but it creates high cardinality. Request IDs and user IDs make so many unique streams that ingestion and query performance suffer and eventually hit configured limits. Loki's cardinality guidance warns against this for good reason.

  • Shrink the time range and guess. This works if you already know roughly when something happened. During an incident, or with a ticket that came in days later, you usually don't.

  • Send some logs to a separate full-text index. That means running a second system, paying to index every field, and making engineers switch tools mid-investigation.

Full-text search removes that tradeoff. The secondary index tells Loki which data can contain a literal string, so Loki reads only that data and skips the rest. That makes a big difference in how much data a query scans and how fast it returns.

And it does this without the overhead of a traditional inverted index. The Logline technology behind it adds approximately 10% to compute costs and 10% to storage at Grafana Cloud scale with the current capabilities. Much of that cost is offset by the query compute Loki saves by reading less data.

Loki also stays schemaless. You keep your labels and your ingestion pipelines, whether that's Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, or another supported client, and you keep writing LogQL. For supported queries, searches that used to time out can now return in seconds or less.

Find answers faster with full-text search 

Full-text search accelerates several LogQL patterns used for needle-in-a-haystack lookups:

  • Exact string matches, using |=.

  • Literal regex searches, using |~, including case-sensitive searches and case-insensitive searches with (?i).

  • Label filter expressions over structured metadata and label attributes, such as | transaction_id="12345".

  • Post-parser literal expressions over extracted attributes, such as | json | transaction_id="12345".

Some advanced regex constructions are not supported; see the full-text search documentation for details.

These patterns above support investigations ranging from following a transaction ID to tracking down an intermittent error. Here’s how faster lookups help engineers and AI agents follow those leads.

Trace one ID across weeks of logs

Most needle-in-a-haystack searches start from a single identifier: a customer ID from a support ticket, a failing transaction from a payment alert, or a trace ID copied from a slow span.

With full-text search, the line filter you already use is the fast path:

{service="payments"} |= "txn-123456"

Loki no longer has to read every chunk in the stream selector across the whole time range. The index sends it to the data that can contain txn-123456. You can search a wider time range with a broader stream selector and still get results fast enough to stay focused.

Anyone on the on-call rotation can paste an ID, set a long time range, and get an answer. You no longer need a Loki expert to make that query efficient.

Hunt down rare and intermittent errors

Some of the hardest incidents to investigate never show up on a dashboard. An error shows up a few times a day on a few hosts, and the only evidence is a specific string buried in the logs.

Full-text search speeds up literal and case-insensitive searches, so you can look across services for rare errors without knowing in advance where they'll appear:

{service="api"} |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You can also combine literals to narrow results while staying on the fast path:

{service="api"} |= "txn-123456" |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You find the first occurrence of an intermittent failure faster, which makes it easier to tie that failure to a deploy, a dependency, or a specific customer.

Speed up AI-driven investigations 

Fast lookups matter even more as AI agents take on more of the investigation work. AI-driven investigations often run many queries in a row: an agent checks a hypothesis, searches for an ID, follows it into another service, and searches again. 

Faster needle-in-a-haystack queries mean each of those steps returns sooner, so the investigation keeps moving.

Get started

If you use Grafana Cloud Logs, full-text search is available now at no additional cost. You don't need to change ingestion, redesign labels, or learn a new query language.

Try full-text search in your stack, or create a free Grafana Cloud account to get started today.  

To run your first search:

  1. Open Explore in your Grafana Cloud stack and choose your Grafana Cloud Logs data source.

  2. Pick a stream selector and add a line filter for a value you'd normally search for, such as a request ID, customer ID, or error string.

  3. Set a longer time range than you'd usually risk, such as the last few days or weeks, and run the query.

For supported query patterns and best practices, see the full-text search documentation.

Faster search is one way we’re helping teams get more value from their logs. At ObservabilityCON 2026, we also announced Adaptive Logs updates to give you more control over storage costs. To learn more, check out this on-demand talk from the event.

title: What's new in Pyroscope: profile more of your workflows, troubleshoot with AI agents, and more
summary:
When an application slows down or memory usage keeps climbing, knowing which code is responsible can help you find a fix faster. Continuous profiling gives you that visibility, so you can see where your application spends resources such as CPU time and memory.

We’ve made updates to Pyroscope, our open source continuous profiling database, that make it easier to profile your applications, find performance bottlenecks, and optimize your code, whether you're doing the work yourself or with an AI agent. 

Highlights include:

  • Profile more of your workloads: Memory profiling for Python and Rust, and .NET support on Windows, helps you find performance bottlenecks across more of your services.

  • Let AI agents work with your profiling data: Pyroscope commands in gcx, the Grafana CLI, let an agent query your profiles directly.

  • See more of your profiling data in Grafana: Exemplars and a new Call Tree view help you explore your profiles visually, whether you're investigating on your own or looking at what an agent found.

Many of these capabilities build directly on Pyroscope 2.0, the ground-up rearchitecture of Pyroscope that makes continuous profiling more cost-effective at scale (in our production environment, it reduced the symbol storage footprint by up to 95%). For example, exemplars require the v2 storage layer that Pyroscope 2.0 is built on. 

Read on to learn more about some of the latest updates. And for a full list of recent changes, see the release notes for Pyroscope and Profiles Drilldown.

Profile more of your workloads

Memory profiling and Windows support have been some of the most frequently requested features for Pyroscope. 

If you run Python or Rust services, you can now use the Pyroscope SDKs to see where their memory goes, not just their CPU time. If you run .NET applications on Windows, you can now profile those, too.

Find memory leaks and heavy allocation: memory profiling for Python

Memory issues can be hard to track down from metrics alone. A container's memory graph shows that usage is climbing, but not which code is allocating that memory. CPU profiles don't answer that either, since they show where your code spends time. Memory profiles show which code paths allocate the most memory and which allocated the memory that's still in use, which is what you need when a service's memory keeps growing, or its allocations drive up garbage collection work.

The Python SDK now supports memory profiling, so you can see which code allocates the most memory and which code allocated the memory that's still in use, alongside the CPU profiles you already collect. Enable it with mem_enabled=True:

pyroscope.configure(
    application_name = "my.python.app",
    server_address   = "http://my-pyroscope-server:4040",
    mem_enabled      = True,
)

To learn more, see the PR and the Python SDK docs.

Find memory leaks and heap growth: memory profiling for Rust

In addition to CPU profiling, the Pyroscope Rust SDK now supports memory profiling through the jemalloc allocator. It reports in-use memory, so you can see which code paths allocated the most live memory and track down heap growth and leaks.

To learn more, see the PR, the Rust SDK docs, and the jemalloc example.

Profile .NET applications on Windows 

If you run .NET applications on Windows, including .NET Framework applications hosted in IIS, you can now send profiles from them to Pyroscope and find hot spots without migrating them first. 

Windows support is for x64, starting with version 1.3.0 of the profiler. On .NET 8, 9, and 10, you get the same profile types on Windows as on Linux, enabled with the same environment variables. On .NET Framework 4.7 and later, CPU and wall-time profiling are available.

To learn more, see the PR and the .NET SDK docs. Note: this feature is currently in public preview. 

Let AI agents work with your profiling data

Without access to your profiles, an AI coding agent can only reason about why a service is slow from the code in front of it, or you have to copy flame graphs and numbers into the conversation by hand. With access to your profiles, it can work from the same data you would, with visibility into which services use the most resources, which functions are responsible, and what a specific profile looked like at a specific time.

gcx, the Grafana CLI, gives you and your AI coding agent structured access to your Grafana instance, from dashboards and alerts to metrics, logs, traces, and profiles. gcx enables agent mode automatically in many coding agents, such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor, and you can enable it yourself for any other agent with --agent. 

gcx now also includes gcx profiles commands for querying Pyroscope. To see gcx in action with Pyroscope, both in the terminal and with an AI agent, watch this community call.

Below are some of the ways you can use gcx with your profiling data, whether you run the commands yourself or an agent runs them for you. You don't need to run your own stack to try them. Grafana Play has demo data you can query, so you can point gcx at it by adding a play context:

gcx config set stacks.play.grafana.server https://play.grafana.org
gcx config set stacks.play.grafana.org-id 1
gcx config set contexts.play.stack play
export GCX_CONTEXT=play

GCX_CONTEXT selects the play context for commands in this terminal session, without changing your default context. The commands below also use the Play profiles data source, grafanacloud-profiles. 

To use your own data, open a new terminal, leave out -d grafanacloud-profiles, and change the service name.

Start with the services using the most resources

When you run many services, it's not always clear which one to look at first. gcx profiles metrics --top ranks your services by a profile type, such as CPU, over a time window, so you or your agent can start with the ones using the most resources:

gcx profiles metrics '{}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h \
  --top

To try this with your AI coding agent and the Grafana Play data, use this prompt:

Using gcx with the play context, find which services used the most CPU over the last hour in the grafanacloud-profiles datasource.

To learn more, see the PR and the gcx profiles metrics CLI reference docs.

Go from the combined view to the exact profile with exemplars

An aggregated profile blends every instance of a service together over the time range, so a single misbehaving process can be hard to spot. Exemplars show individual profiles ranked by their value for the profile type you query, such as CPU time or memory, so you or your agent can go straight to the most expensive ones and see what happened in each, instead of only the combined total.

gcx profiles exemplars lists the most expensive individual profiles, and you can pass one of their profile IDs to gcx profiles query to see the top functions in just that profile:

gcx profiles exemplars profile '{service_name="checkoutservice"}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h

gcx profiles query '{service_name="checkoutservice"}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h \
  --profile-id

If your profiles are linked to traces, you can also narrow a query to a single span or trace to see the code that ran during a slow operation or request.

To try this with your AI coding agent and the Grafana Play data, use this prompt:

Use exemplars to find the most expensive CPU profile for checkoutservice in the grafanacloud-profiles datasource in the last hour, and summarize its most CPU-intensive functions.

To learn more, see the PRs for exemplars, profile IDs, and span and trace selectors. Also see the exemplars CLI reference docs and query CLI reference docs.

Export profiles to use with other tools

Sometimes you want the raw profile: to open it in tools you already use, to attach it to an issue, or to keep a snapshot from before a change so you can compare later. Add -o pprof to gcx profiles query to download the profile as a pprof file, which you can open with go tool pprof.

You can also start from the Grafana UI. With the release of Profiles Drilldown 3.0 in October, you can click the Export profile data download icon above the flame graph and select gcx command, which copies a gcx profiles query command that downloads the profile you're looking at as a pprof file. pyroscope.configure(

)

title: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience
summary:
Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7.

We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. 

In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below.

Starting with why

“Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella Meadows

At Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible.

Meanwhile, over the last year, the product design team has worked with our engineers to build new interaction patterns to support AI solutions like Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace. Building these patterns opened the door to curiosity, and we started experimenting with new visual forms, colors, shapes, and effects that laid the groundwork for the refresh.

Through this work, our approach to UI style and aesthetics evolved, and so did our purpose: alongside supporting new workflows and use cases, we wanted to bring greater consistency to interactions and design patterns across Grafana. This refresh is the first step toward that goal.

Visual styling and usability

“The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its usefulness.” – Dieter Rams

So why invest in visual styling? To stay relevant? To facilitate sales conversations? Because it looks cool?

All of those reasons are valid, but at Grafana Labs, product designers are utilitarians first. We believe digital products should exist with a clear purpose and function in mind. We think each color, font style, and line should establish a clear information hierarchy and help users quickly understand what's on the page, ultimately making our product easier to use.

As more workflows shift to terminals and agentic chat interfaces, we believe investing in visual style now is foundational to Grafana’s future usability. When fewer user journeys rely on a traditional UI, those that do must emphasize clarity and consistency.

What’s new: a closer look 

This first phase of the refresh focuses on making the Grafana UI clearer and more consistent across workflows and components, while giving you time to adapt to the changes. Here are some of the highlights:

  • New default light and dark themes: These themes use completely new color palettes with improved accessibility compliance by design.

  • Increased consistency across components: We have started to reduce the amount of available UI components and their variants. This means users only need to learn an interaction or a pattern once, and can then leverage it across the entire platform.

  • New font styles, borders, and shadows: By overhauling our visual primitives to work in a proportional and scalable way, we create layers of hierarchy and visual information. As part of our audits, we noticed that many areas of the UI competed for users’ attention. We’re moving to a state where you can immediately understand what’s most important on a page, so you can complete tasks faster and more efficiently. You’ll notice these changes across the building blocks of Grafana, including cards, panels, and drawers.

We’re rolling out the visual refresh gradually so Grafana contributors and users have time to adapt without disrupting critical workflows. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Existing navigation stays the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. 

To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous styling at any time.

For a full list of changes in the public preview, please visit our documentation.

Curiosity, monitoring, and feedback

"There are three key practices needed in order to build and maintain a circle of competence: curiosity and a desire to learn, monitoring, and feedback." – Shane Parrish & Rhiannon Beaubien

Curiosity is a key attribute of product designers at Grafana Labs and we knew that unifying the look and feel across Grafana meant making choices that could elicit strong reactions. This is why learning, gathering feedback, and monitoring the response have been central to our process.

We could have spent a year working on what we think is a perfect new visual styling, running hundreds of internal iterations, but instead we started with early internal dogfooding of the refreshed UI. This led to honest discussions and opinions from Grafanistas across the company, helping us iterate the visual refresh rapidly into a version we could not have achieved without working openly. 

Now, with the refresh in public preview, your feedback is central to how we’ll continue to refine our visual styling. Through our community Slack and a temporary in-app survey, you can tell us directly what’s working, what needs improvement, and what we might have missed. We monitor and discuss this feedback in the open, helping to amplify your voice and share it across the organization. Your responses will be integral to shaping future iterations of the refresh.

We can’t wait to hear what you think, and to continue our evolution toward a bolder visual experience for all Grafana users.

title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
summary:
Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.

And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state.

Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock?

For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.

Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?

The TL;DR on Watchers

Watchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.

Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:

  • The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.

  • The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.

  • The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.

  • The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.

Put the intelligence only where it's needed

Keeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: 

  1. Working out what to watch and what normal looks like

  2. Comparing the same signals with normal again and again

  3. Deciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone for

Only the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. 

Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. 

So a watcher splits the work three ways:

Job

Who does it

When

Decide what to watch and what normal looks like

A calibration agent, with a capable model and tools

Once, and again when you recalibrate

Fetch the data and compare it with the baseline

Plain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern tracking

Every run

Decide whether it matters, and explain why

A small, fast model, in a single call with no tools

Every run

And here's what that workflow looks like:

Calibration: do the hard thinking once

Calibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.

The calibration agent:

  • Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"

  • Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.

  • Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.

  • Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.

A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.

Run plain code, then make one model call

A calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:

  • Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.

  • Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.

  • Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.

Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.

For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.

We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.

What it costs

Here's what that adds up to for the 43 Watchers running on our internal stack, at our list price of $2 per million tokens:

Types of Watchers

Cost to run per month

Median Watcher

Less than $5

41 of 43 Watchers

Less than $10

Most expensive Watcher (43 checks, every 15 minutes)

A little over $20

Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.

And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state.

Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock?

For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.

Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?

The TL;DR on Watchers

Watchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.

Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:

  • The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.

  • The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.

  • The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.

  • The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.

Put the intelligence only where it's needed

Keeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: 

  1. Working out what to watch and what normal looks like

  2. Comparing the same signals with normal again and again

  3. Deciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone for

Only the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. 

Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't.

Calibration: do the hard thinking once

Calibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.

The calibration agent:

  • Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"

  • Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.

  • Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.

  • Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.

A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.

A calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:

  • Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.

  • Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.

  • Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.

Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.

For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.

We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.
